p.src: Now in the first month of spring, in the second year of Zhangwu, General of the Rear Huang Zhong of Wuwei accompanied the First Emperor on his campaign against Wu; when he suddenly heard the First Emperor say that old generals were of no use, he took up his sword, mounted his horse, and with five or six personal attendants rode straight to the camp at Yiling. Wu Ban, Zhang Nan, and Feng Xi received him and asked, “What has brought you here, old general?” Huang Zhong replied, “Ever since I followed His Majesty from Changsha, I have rendered long and arduous service. Though I am now past seventy, I can eat ten jin of meat, draw a two-shi bow, and ride a horse capable of a thousand li; I am not yet old. Yesterday His Majesty said that we old men were useless, so I have come to engage Eastern Wu. Watch me slay their generals, and judge whether I am old or not!”

p.src: As they were speaking, a sudden report came that the vanguard of Wu had arrived and its scouts were approaching the camp. Huang Zhong sprang up in high spirits, left the tent, and mounted his horse. Feng Xi and the others urged him, “Old general, please do not advance rashly.” Huang Zhong would not listen and galloped away. Wu Ban ordered Feng Xi to lead troops to support him. Before the Wu battle line, Huang Zhong reined in his horse, held his sword crosswise, and challenged the vanguard commander Pan Zhang to single combat. Pan Zhang sent his subordinate commander Shi Ji out on horseback. Taking Huang Zhong lightly because of his age, Shi Ji leveled his spear and rode out to fight; but before three bouts had passed, Huang Zhong cut him down from his horse with a single stroke. Pan Zhang flew into a rage and came to fight Huang Zhong, brandishing the Green Dragon blade once wielded by Lord Guan. They crossed horses for several bouts, with neither gaining the advantage. Huang Zhong fought with all his might and terrible ferocity. Pan Zhang, realizing he was no match for him, wheeled his horse and fled. Huang Zhong pressed the advantage in pursuit and returned completely victorious. On the road he encountered Guan Xing and Zhang Bao. Guan Xing said, “We have come by imperial command to assist you, old general. Now that you have won your victory, please return to camp at once.” Huang Zhong would not listen.

p.src: The next day, Pan Zhang came again to issue a challenge. Huang Zhong mounted his horse eagerly. Guan Xing and Zhang Bao wished to assist him, but Huang Zhong refused; Wu Ban also wished to assist him, but Huang Zhong refused him as well; he led out only five thousand troops himself to meet the enemy. Before many bouts had been fought, Pan Zhang trailed his blade and fled. Huang Zhong spurred his horse in pursuit and shouted fiercely, “Do not flee, rebel general! Today I shall avenge Lord Guan!” After he had pursued for more than thirty li, mighty shouts erupted on every side and the ambushing troops emerged all at once. Zhou Tai was on the right, Han Dang on the left, Pan Zhang before him, and Ling Tong behind, trapping Huang Zhong in their midst. Suddenly a violent wind arose. As Huang Zhong hastened to retreat, Ma Zhong appeared on the hillside leading a body of troops and shot an arrow into Huang Zhong’s shoulder, almost knocking him from his horse. Seeing Huang Zhong struck by an arrow, the troops of Wu attacked him together. Suddenly great shouts arose from the rear and two columns charged in. The Wu troops scattered, and Huang Zhong was rescued—it was Guan Xing and Zhang Bao. The two young generals escorted Huang Zhong straight to the imperial camp. Huang Zhong was old and weak of blood; the arrow wound throbbed and split with pain, and his condition became grave. The First Emperor came in person to see him, stroked his back, and said, “That you should be wounded, old general, is my fault!” Huang Zhong said, “Your servant is merely a common warrior, yet I was fortunate enough to encounter Your Majesty. This year I am seventy-five; I have lived long enough. I pray that Your Majesty will take good care of your imperial person and seek to recover the Central Plain!” When he had finished speaking, he lost consciousness, and that night he died in the imperial camp. A later poet lamented him in verse:

p.src: When the First Emperor saw that Huang Zhong had breathed his last, his grief knew no end. He ordered a coffin and outer casket prepared and had him buried at Chengdu. The First Emperor sighed, “Of the Five Tiger Generals, three have already died. Yet I have still been unable to avenge them. How deeply painful it is!” He then led the Imperial Guard straight to Xiaoting, assembled all his generals, divided the army into eight columns, and advanced by both land and water. He ordered Huang Quan to command the forces by water, while he himself led the main army forward by land. It was the middle of the second month in the second year of Zhangwu.

p.src: When Han Dang and Zhou Tai heard that the First Emperor had personally come to campaign against them, they led out troops to meet him. When the two armies had drawn up opposite each other, Han Dang and Zhou Tai rode out. At the gateway of the Shu camp they saw the First Emperor emerge in person, surrounded before and behind by a yellow silk parasol embroidered in gold, white yak-tail standards and a yellow battle-axe on either side, and ceremonial insignia of gold and silver. Han Dang shouted, “Your Majesty is now sovereign of Shu. Why do you lightly expose yourself? Should some mishap occur, regret would come too late!” Pointing at him from afar, the First Emperor cursed, “You dogs of Wu have harmed one who was as my own hands and feet. I swear I shall not share heaven and earth with you!” Han Dang turned to the assembled generals and asked, “Who dares charge the Shu troops?” His subordinate commander Xia Xun leveled his spear and rode out. From behind the First Emperor, Zhang Bao leveled his eighteen-foot spear, spurred his horse forward, and with a tremendous shout charged straight at Xia Xun. Hearing Zhang Bao’s voice thunder like a mighty peal, Xia Xun was seized with fear; just as he was about to flee, Zhou Ping, Zhou Tai’s younger brother, saw that Xia Xun could not hold his own and came galloping up with his sword. Seeing this, Guan Xing urged his horse forward with sword in hand to meet him. With a mighty shout, Zhang Bao thrust his spear into Xia Xun and sent him tumbling from his horse. Zhou Ping was so astonished that he had no time to react, and Guan Xing cut him down with a single stroke. The two young generals then charged at Han Dang and Zhou Tai, who hastily retreated into their ranks. Watching them, the First Emperor sighed, “A tiger father does not beget a dog for a son!” He pointed with his imperial whip, and the Shu troops surged forward together, inflicting a crushing defeat on the army of Wu. The eight columns poured forward like welling springs, slaughtering the Wu army until corpses covered the fields and blood flowed in rivers.

p.src: Now Gan Ning was recuperating from illness aboard a ship. Hearing that the Shu army had arrived in great force, he hurriedly mounted his horse and presently encountered a fierce band of tribal warriors, all with loose hair and bare feet, armed with bows, crossbows, long spears, shields, swords, and axes; at their head was the tribal king Shamoke, whose face was as red as blood and whose blue-green eyes bulged from their sockets. He wielded an iron spiked mace and wore two bows at his waist, presenting a fearsome sight. Seeing the strength of his force, Gan Ning dared not engage and wheeled his horse to flee; but Shamoke shot an arrow into his head. Gan Ning fled with the arrow still lodged in him. Reaching Fuchikou, he sat beneath a great tree and died. Hundreds of crows in the tree gathered around his corpse. When the King of Wu heard of it, he grieved without end, buried Gan Ning with full honors, and established a temple in which sacrifices were offered to him. A later poet lamented him in verse:

p.src: Meanwhile, the First Emperor pressed the pursuit and thereby captured Xiaoting. The troops of Wu fled in all directions. When the First Emperor recalled his troops, Guan Xing alone was nowhere to be seen. Alarmed, he ordered Zhang Bao and the others to search for him in every direction. It turned out that Guan Xing had fought his way into the Wu ranks, where he encountered his enemy Pan Zhang and spurred his horse after him. Pan Zhang was terrified and fled into a mountain valley, where he disappeared from sight. Guan Xing supposed he must still be somewhere in the mountains and searched back and forth, but could not find him. Night gradually fell, and he lost both his bearings and the road. Fortunately, the stars and moon gave light. He made his way into a remote part of the mountains; by then it was the second watch. Coming to a country house, he dismounted and knocked at the gate. An old man came out and asked who he was. Guan Xing replied, “I am a warrior who lost his way and came here. I beg a meal to satisfy my hunger.” The old man led him inside. Guan Xing saw bright candles burning in the hall, and in its central place hung a painted image of Lord Guan. Guan Xing burst into tears and bowed before it. The old man asked, “General, why do you weep and bow?” Guan Xing replied, “This is my father.” Hearing this, the old man immediately bowed down before Guan Xing. Guan Xing asked, “Why do you venerate my father?” The old man answered, “All this region lies under the protection of your honored father’s divine spirit. Every household served him while he lived; how much more should we do so now that he has become a god? This old man has wished only that the Shu army might soon avenge him. Now that you have come, General, the people here are blessed indeed.” He then set out wine to entertain Guan Xing, removed the saddle, and fed his horse.

p.src: After the third watch, another man suddenly knocked at the gate. The old man went out to question him and found that it was the Wu general Pan Zhang, who had also come seeking lodging. The moment Pan Zhang entered the thatched hall, Guan Xing saw him, gripped his sword, and thundered, “Traitorous villain, do not flee!” Pan Zhang turned and made for the door. But suddenly a man appeared outside the gate, his face dark red as a ripe jujube, with phoenix eyes, silkworm brows, and three flowing strands of handsome beard; clad in a green robe and golden armor, he entered with one hand upon his sword. Seeing that it was Lord Guan manifesting his divine presence, Pan Zhang gave one great cry, and his wits fled in terror; before he could turn, Guan Xing’s sword had risen and fallen, striking him dead. Guan Xing cut out his heart, drained its blood, and offered it in sacrifice before Lord Guan’s sacred image. Having recovered his father’s Green Dragon Crescent Blade, Guan Xing hung Pan Zhang’s head beneath his horse’s neck, bade the old man farewell, mounted Pan Zhang’s horse, and set off toward his own camp. The old man himself dragged out Pan Zhang’s corpse and burned it.

p.src: Now Guan Xing had traveled many miles when he suddenly heard men shouting and horses neighing, and a body of troops came toward him; the officer at their head was Ma Zhong, one of Pan Zhang’s subordinates. Ma Zhong saw that Guan Xing had slain his commander Pan Zhang and hung the man’s head beneath his horse’s neck; and that Guan Xing had also recovered the Green Dragon Blade; he flew into a rage, spurred his horse, and charged Guan Xing. Seeing in Ma Zhong one of his father’s mortal enemies, Guan Xing’s fury rose to the heavens; he raised the Green Dragon Blade and struck at him. Ma Zhong’s three hundred soldiers surged forward together and, with a mighty shout, surrounded Guan Xing at the heart of the field. Alone and outnumbered, Guan Xing was in grave danger. Suddenly another body of troops charged in from the northwest: it was Zhang Bao. Seeing reinforcements arrive, Ma Zhong hastily led his troops away. Guan Xing and Zhang Bao pursued together. Before they had gone several miles, Mi Fang and Fu Shiren appeared ahead with troops, searching for Ma Zhong. The two forces joined, and a confused battle ensued. Zhang Bao and Guan Xing had too few men, so they hastily withdrew. Returning to Xiaoting, they appeared before the First Sovereign, presented the head, and related the whole affair. The First Sovereign marveled and rewarded the three armies.

p.src: Meanwhile, Ma Zhong returned to Han Dang and Zhou Tai. They gathered the defeated troops and divided up the defense among themselves. Countless soldiers had been wounded. Ma Zhong encamped with Fu Shiren and Mi Fang on an islet in the river. At the third watch that night, the soldiers’ weeping continued without cease. Mi Fang listened secretly and heard one group say, “We are all soldiers of Jingzhou. Through Lü Meng’s treachery, our lord lost his life. Now Imperial Uncle Liu has personally led an expedition here, and sooner or later Eastern Wu is finished. The ones we hate are Mi Fang and Fu Shiren. Why do we not kill those two traitors and surrender at the Shu camp? It would earn us no small merit.” Another group of soldiers said, “Do not be hasty. Let us wait for an opening and then strike.” When Mi Fang had heard all this, he was greatly alarmed and consulted Fu Shiren: “The army’s loyalty is wavering. Our lives can scarcely be preserved. The man the ruler of Shu hates most now is Ma Zhong alone; why not kill him, take his head to the ruler of Shu, and declare, ‘We had no choice but to surrender to Wu. Now that we know Your Majesty has come, we have journeyed especially to your camp to beg forgiveness’?” Fu Shiren said, “No. If we go, disaster will surely befall us.” Mi Fang said, “The ruler of Shu is generous, humane, and virtuous; and Crown Prince Adou is now my nephew. If he but remembers that I am of the imperial kin, he will surely be unwilling to harm me.”

p.src: Their plan settled, the two first prepared their horses. At the third watch, they entered Ma Zhong’s tent and stabbed him to death, cut off his head, and rode straight for Xiaoting with several dozen horsemen. The soldiers guarding the approaches first escorted them to Zhang Nan and Feng Xi, to whom they related the whole affair. The next day, they entered the imperial camp, appeared before the First Sovereign, and presented Ma Zhong’s head. Weeping, they pleaded, “Your servants truly never harbored thoughts of rebellion; Lü Meng deceived us by claiming Lord Guan was already dead, tricked us into opening the city gates, and left us no choice but to surrender. Now, hearing that Your Sacred Majesty had come, we killed this villain especially to avenge Your Majesty’s grievance. We prostrate ourselves and beg Your Majesty to pardon our crimes.” The First Sovereign said in great anger, “I left Chengdu long ago. Why did you two not come then to confess your crimes? Only now, seeing yourselves in peril, have you come with artful words to save your lives! If I spare you, how could I face Lord Guan beneath the Nine Springs?” When he had finished speaking, he ordered Guan Xing to erect a spirit tablet for Lord Guan in the imperial camp. The First Sovereign personally carried Ma Zhong’s head before it and offered sacrifice. He then ordered Guan Xing to strip Mi Fang and Fu Shiren, make them kneel before the spirit tablet, and personally slice them to death as an offering to Lord Guan. Suddenly Zhang Bao came before the tent, knelt weeping, and said, “The enemies of my second uncle have all been executed; but on what day shall my father’s wrong be avenged?” The First Sovereign said, “Worthy nephew, do not grieve. I shall pacify all Jiangnan and slaughter every dog of Wu. I will make certain those two villains are captured and let you mince them with your own hands as a sacrifice to your father.” Zhang Bao tearfully gave thanks and withdrew.

Sun Quan grew fearful and assembled his civil and military officers for counsel. Bu Zhi memorialized, “Those whom the ruler of Shu hated were Lü Meng, Pan Zhang, Ma Zhong, Mi Fang, and Fu Shiren. All these men are now dead. Only Fan Qiang and Zhang Da remain here in Eastern Wu. Why not seize these two, send them back together with Zhang Fei’s head, hand Jingzhou over to Shu, return the Lady, submit a memorial seeking peace, renew our former friendship, and join in a common plan to destroy Wei? Then the Shu army will withdraw of its own accord.” Sun Quan accepted his advice. He had an aloeswood casket prepared and Zhang Fei’s head placed within it, bound Fan Qiang and Zhang Da, and imprisoned them in a caged cart. He then appointed Cheng Bing as envoy and sent him toward Xiaoting bearing a letter of state.

p.src: Now the First Sovereign was about to order his army to advance. Suddenly a close attendant reported, “Eastern Wu has sent an envoy bearing the head of General of Chariots and Cavalry Zhang, together with the imprisoned villains Fan Qiang and Zhang Da.” The First Sovereign raised both hands to his brow and said, “This is a gift from Heaven, wrought also by the spirit of my third brother!” He immediately ordered Zhang Bao to erect Zhang Fei’s spirit tablet. When the First Sovereign saw Zhang Fei’s head in the casket, its countenance unchanged, he burst into loud weeping. Zhang Bao himself took up a keen blade and put Fan Qiang and Zhang Da to death by the lingering death of ten thousand cuts, offering them to his father’s spirit. When the sacrifice was over, the First Sovereign’s anger remained unabated, and he was resolved to destroy Wu. Ma Liang memorialized, “All your enemies have now been executed, and your grievance may be considered avenged. The Wu officer Cheng Bing has come, wishing to return Jingzhou, send the Lady home, bind the alliance forever, and join us in a common plan to destroy Wei. He awaits Your Sacred Majesty’s decree.” The First Sovereign said angrily, “The enemy against whom I grind my teeth is Sun Quan himself. If I now make peace and alliance with him, I shall betray the oath I once swore with my second brother. First I shall destroy Wu; then I shall destroy Wei.” He was about to execute the envoy and sever all relations with Wu. Only the earnest pleas of many officers secured the envoy’s pardon. Cheng Bing fled back in abject terror and reported to the ruler of Wu, “Shu refuses to discuss peace and has sworn first to destroy Eastern Wu and then attack Wei. His officers remonstrated bitterly, but he would not listen. What are we to do?”

p.src: Sun Quan was greatly alarmed and lost his composure. Kan Ze stepped forward and memorialized, “A pillar capable of upholding heaven is at hand—why not employ him?” Sun Quan urgently asked whom he meant. Kan Ze said, “In former days, all the great affairs of Eastern Wu were entrusted to Zhou Yu; afterward, Lu Su succeeded him; and after Lu Su died, decisions rested with Lü Meng. Now, though Lü Meng too is dead, Lu Xun remains in Jingzhou. Though known as a scholar, he possesses truly heroic talent and far-reaching strategy. In my judgment, he is no less able than Zhou Yu. When Lord Guan was defeated, every stratagem came from Lu Xun. If Your Majesty will employ him, Shu will surely be defeated. Should anything go amiss, I am willing to share his punishment.” Sun Quan said, “But for your words, Derun, I would have ruined our great undertaking.” Zhang Zhao said, “Lu Xun is merely a scholar and no match for Liu Bei; I fear he cannot be employed.” Gu Yong also said, “Lu Xun is young and of little standing; I fear the senior officers will not submit to him. If they refuse, disorder will arise and the great undertaking will surely be imperiled.” Bu Zhi likewise said, “Lu Xun’s abilities suffice only to govern a commandery. It would be unfitting to entrust him with so great a charge.” Kan Ze cried aloud, “If Lu Xun is not employed, Eastern Wu is finished! I will stake my whole family upon him!” Sun Quan said, “I too have long known Lu Xun to be a man of extraordinary talent. My mind is made up. Say no more.”

p.src: He therefore ordered Lu Xun to be summoned. Lu Xun had originally been named Lu Yi, but later changed his name to Xun; his courtesy name was Boyan, and he was a native of Wu County in Wu Commandery. He was the grandson of Lu Yu, Gate Commandant under the Han, and the son of Lu Jun, Commandant of Jiujiang. He stood eight chi tall, and his face was as fair as fine jade. He held the office of General Who Pacifies the West. He came at once in obedience to the summons. When he had finished paying homage, Sun Quan said, “The troops of Shu now press upon our borders. I specially appoint you to command all our forces and defeat Liu Bei.” Lu Xun said, “The civil and military officers of Jiangdong are all Your Majesty’s veteran retainers. I am young and without ability—how could I command them?” Sun Quan said, “Kan Derun has pledged his whole family for you, and I too have long known your abilities. I now appoint you Chief Commander. Do not decline.” Lu Xun said, “What if the civil and military officers refuse to obey?” Sun Quan took off the sword he wore and gave it to him, saying, “If any disobey your commands, execute them first and report afterward.” Lu Xun said, “Having received so weighty a trust, how dare I refuse the appointment? I ask only that Your Majesty assemble all the officers tomorrow and then bestow the sword upon me.” Kan Ze said, “In ancient times, when a general was appointed, an altar was always raised and the officers assembled; he was granted the white yak-tail standard, the yellow battle-axe, the seals and ribbons, and the military tallies. Only then did his authority prevail and his commands command awe. Your Majesty should now follow that rite: choose an auspicious day, raise an altar, appoint Lu Xun Chief Commander, and grant him the emblems of plenipotentiary authority. Then none will dare disobey.” Sun Quan followed his advice. He ordered an altar completed overnight, assembled all the officials, and invited Lu Xun to ascend it. There he appointed him Chief Commander, Right Protector of the Army, and General Who Pacifies the West; advanced him to Marquis of Lou; bestowed upon him a jeweled sword and seal-ribbon; and placed under his command the forces of the six commanderies and eighty-one prefectures, together with all the armies of Jing and Chu. The King of Wu charged him, “Within the palace gates, I shall rule; beyond them, the general shall command.”

p.src: Lu Xun accepted the command and descended from the altar. Zhou Tai said, “At present, Sun Huan, General Who Pacifies the East and our lord’s nephew, is besieged within the city of Yiling, with no provisions inside and no relief force outside. I ask the Chief Commander to devise a sound plan without delay, rescue Sun Huan, and set our lord’s mind at ease.” Lu Xun said, “I have long known that General Sun enjoys the wholehearted support of his troops and can certainly hold fast. p.src: The next day, Lu Xun issued orders that every general defend his assigned position, hold the strategic passes firmly, and not engage the enemy rashly. They all mocked him for cowardice and were unwilling to remain on the defensive. The following day, Lu Xun took his seat in the command tent, summoned the generals, and said, “By the king’s honored command, I have assumed supreme command of the armies. Yesterday I repeatedly and explicitly ordered each of you to hold your positions firmly, yet none of you obeyed me. Why?” Han Dang said, “Ever since I followed General Sun in pacifying Jiangnan, I have fought in hundreds of battles. As for the other generals, some followed the General Who Attacks Rebels, while others have served our present king; all are warriors who have donned stout armor, grasped sharp weapons, and braved death. Now our lord has made you Chief Commander and ordered you to drive back the troops of Shu. You should quickly settle upon a plan, deploy the forces, and advance by separate routes to accomplish our great purpose. Instead, you merely order us to hold fast and not fight. Do you mean to wait for Heaven itself to slay the enemy? I am no man who clings to life and fears death. Why do you make us lose our fighting spirit?” At this, all the generals in the tent cried in agreement, “General Han speaks truly. We are ready to fight to the death!” When Lu Xun had heard them out, he drew his sword and held it in his hand, then said sternly, “Though I am but a humble scholar, our lord has entrusted me with this grave responsibility because I possess some small merit and am able to endure humiliation and shoulder heavy burdens. Each of you must guard his pass and hold the strategic positions firmly. You are not permitted to move rashly. Whoever violates this order will be executed!” The generals all withdrew in anger and resentment.

p.src: When Han Dang saw the First Ruler’s forces approaching, he sent a man to inform Lu Xun. Fearing that Han Dang might act rashly, Lu Xun hurried over on a swift horse to inspect the situation. He found Han Dang mounted upon a hill, gazing into the distance as the troops of Shu advanced over mountains and fields; amid their ranks, a yellow silk imperial canopy could be dimly seen. Han Dang received Lu Xun, and the two watched side by side on horseback. Pointing, Han Dang said, “Liu Bei must be there among the troops. I wish to attack him.” Lu Xun said, “Liu Bei has raised his army and marched east, winning more than ten battles in succession. His momentum is now at its height. For now, we must hold the heights and defend the difficult ground. We must not venture out lightly, for if we do, the outcome will be unfavorable. We should merely encourage the officers and men, spread our defenses widely, and watch for a change in his disposition. At present, he ranges freely over broad plains and open country, flushed with success. If we hold firm and refuse to emerge, he will be unable to obtain battle and will surely move his camps among wooded hills. Then I shall defeat him with an extraordinary stratagem.” Though Han Dang assented aloud, in his heart he remained wholly unconvinced.

p.src: The First Emperor sent his vanguard forward to challenge the enemy, hurling every manner of abuse at them. Lu Xun ordered his men to stop their ears and pay no heed, and forbade them to go out and engage. He personally toured every pass and strategic gateway, reassuring the officers and men and commanding them all to hold firm. When the First Emperor saw that the troops of Wu would not come out, he grew impatient. Ma Liang said, “Lu Xun is deeply versed in strategy. Your Majesty has come from afar to wage this campaign, and it has already lasted from spring into summer. His refusal to come out is intended to await some change in our army. I beg Your Majesty to consider this carefully.” The First Emperor said, “What scheme could he have? He merely fears his enemy. Having suffered defeat several times before, how would he dare come out again now?” Feng Xi, commander of the vanguard, memorialized, “The weather is now fiercely hot. The army is encamped amid scorching heat, and fetching water is extremely difficult.” The First Emperor accordingly ordered every camp to move to places thick with mountain woods, close to streams and beside ravines, there to wait until summer had passed and autumn arrived, when they would combine their strength and advance. Feng Xi obeyed the command and moved all the camps into places densely shaded by trees. Ma Liang memorialized, “If our army moves and the troops of Wu suddenly descend upon us, what shall we do?” The First Emperor replied, “I shall order Wu Ban to lead more than ten thousand of our weaker troops and encamp on level ground near the Wu stockade. I shall personally select eight thousand elite soldiers and conceal them in the mountain valleys. When Lu Xun learns that I have moved camp, he is certain to seize the opportunity and attack; Wu Ban shall then feign defeat. If Lu Xun pursues him, I shall lead my troops out in a sudden attack and cut off his retreat. Then the young whelp will be ours to capture.” The civil and military officers all offered their congratulations, saying, “Your Majesty’s divine foresight and marvelous calculations are beyond any of us!”
